definition: To deflower someone; to take a person's virginity through first penetrative intercourse, typically framed from the penetrating partner's perspective.
notes: Phrasal infinitive. Formal/literary register; sounds dated in contemporary spoken Russian. The nominalised form лишение девственности (defloration) is equally formal.

definition: Russian Cyrillic rendering of the English acronym BDSM (bondage, discipline, dominance, submission, sadism, masochism); umbrella term for consensual power-exchange and pain-play practices.
notes: Each Cyrillic letter maps phonetically to the English initial. Recognised primarily among younger urban Russians and internet users; awareness has grown sharply since 2010s social media.

definition: Sadomasochism; sexual gratification derived from both inflicting and receiving pain, humiliation, or domination.
notes: Standard clinical loanword from German/French via English. Widely used in both clinical psychology and popular journalism. The abbreviated form СМ (SM) is also current in subculture contexts.

definition: Sadism; sexual or non-sexual gratification from inflicting pain, humiliation, or suffering on another; named after the Marquis de Sade.
notes: Extremely widely known; routinely used in everyday Russian for any pleasure in cruelty, not just sexual. This non-sexual broadening is parallel to English usage.

definition: Masochism; sexual gratification derived from experiencing pain, humiliation, or subjugation; named after Leopold von Sacher-Masoch.
notes: Also used figuratively in Russian for apparently self-destructive or pointless suffering ('зачем ты это терпишь — чистый мазохизм'). High general recognition due to figurative use.

definition: Fetishism; a paraphilia in which sexual arousal is systematically triggered by a specific object, body part, or non-sexual material.
notes: The -изм suffix marks the clinical/pathological framing, distinguishing it from the more colloquial standalone noun фетиш. Used in DSM-aligned psychiatric discourse in Russia.

definition: A fetish; a specific object, body part, or scenario that triggers sexual arousal; colloquially, any strong sexual fixation or kink.
notes: More casual and widely used than фетишизм. Also used non-sexually (e.g., 'у него фетиш на дорогие часы'), exactly mirroring English colloquial extension.

definition: Pedophilia; primary or exclusive sexual attraction to prepubescent children; universally condemned and criminalised.
notes: High crude score reflects extreme moral repugnance despite clinical register — the word itself is technical but denotes a maximally taboo act. Near-universal recognition across all Russian demographics.

definition: Zoophilia; sexual attraction to or sexual contact with animals.
notes: Clinical loanword. Distinct in register from the cruder скотоложество (skotolozhstvo), which is the traditional Russian legal and pejorative term for the physical act.

definition: Necrophilia; sexual attraction to or sexual acts performed with a human corpse.
notes: Clinical loanword; also used figuratively in Russian political discourse for morbid attachment to Soviet-era institutions or ideology ('политическая некрофилия').

definition: Exhibitionism; a paraphilia involving sexual pleasure from exposing one's genitals to non-consenting strangers or from performing sexually in public.
notes: Long and formal; rarely used in casual speech. The person is called эксгибиционист. Non-sexual exhibitionism (showing off) uses the same word in Russian, requiring context to disambiguate.

definition: Voyeurism; sexual pleasure derived from watching others engaged in intimate or sexual behaviour without their knowledge or consent.
notes: Loanword from French via English. The person is вуайерист. More clinical and less known than подглядывание ('peeping'), which is the everyday Russian term for the behaviour.

definition: Bondage; the erotic practice of physically restraining a partner with rope, cuffs, or other materials for sexual arousal or power-exchange purposes.
notes: Direct phonetic loanword from English, pronounced approximately 'bon-DAZH'. Has largely displaced native circumlocutions. Recognition weighted toward younger urban Russians and internet-active populations.

definition: Dominant; a person who takes the controlling, authoritative role in a BDSM dynamic.
notes: The native Russian word доминант exists in non-sexual contexts (music theory, genetics), but this specific BDSM person-noun is a calque of English subculture usage. Not widely understood outside BDSM-aware circles.

definition: Submissive; a person who yields control and power to a dominant partner in BDSM activity.
notes: Direct phonetic loanword from English; recognised almost exclusively within BDSM subculture. The form субмиссивный (adjectival) is also used. Lower recognition than доминант reflects deeper subculture embedding.

definition: Master; in BDSM, the dominant partner in a Master/slave (M/s) dynamic, implying total authority and ongoing ownership of the slave partner.
notes: Native Russian word (craftsman/master) repurposed for BDSM M/s dynamics. Implies a more absolute and continuous power exchange than generic доминант, which may be scene-limited. Low crude score because the word itself is ordinary.

definition: Slave; in BDSM, the submissive partner in a Master/slave (M/s) dynamic, implying total surrender of autonomy to the dominant.
notes: Native Russian word (serf/slave) repurposed for BDSM. Distinct from субмиссив: implies total power exchange (TPE) and an ongoing relationship identity rather than scene-specific submission. The historical weight of крепостное право (serfdom) gives the word extra cultural resonance in Russian.

definition: Mistress; in BDSM, the title and role of a female dominant, used both as an honorific form of address and as a role descriptor.
notes: Standard Russian honorific (polite address for a woman, equivalent to 'Madam/Ms.') repurposed as a BDSM title. The dual register creates a productive ambiguity — the word carries authority even outside kink contexts, which is part of its appeal as a dominant title.

definition: Flogging or caning; in sexual contexts, BDSM impact play involving striking with an implement such as a belt, rod, or strap.
notes: Native Russian word with a primary historical meaning of corporal punishment (school, judicial, or domestic). In BDSM it denotes implement-based impact play, which makes it somewhat more severe in implication than English 'spanking', which defaults to hand strikes.

definition: Slaps or smacks; in sexual contexts, erotic open-hand spanking, typically on the buttocks.
notes: Diminutive/colloquial plural of шлепок (a slap). More playful and lighter in connotation than порка; the diminutive suffix reduces severity. The closest English equivalent is 'light spanking' rather than 'flogging'.

definition: Golden shower; the sexual act of urinating on a partner for erotic gratification.
notes: Direct calque of English 'golden shower'; the same metaphor (urine as gold-coloured rain) was independently or derivatively adopted. Recognition boosted significantly by high-profile political scandal coverage circa 2017.

definition: Coprophilia; sexual arousal or gratification associated with feces or defecation.
notes: Clinical Greek-derived loanword. Lower recognition than most paraphilias in this list because the topic is strongly taboo in Russian public discourse, limiting its appearance even in journalism and popular psychology.

definition: Role-playing games; in sexual contexts, sexual roleplay in which partners enact fantasy scenarios, characters, or personas.
notes: Native phrase (literally 'role-playing games') used in both tabletop gaming and sexual contexts; usage disambiguated by context. Mapped to bdsm_play as the closest registry concept, but ролевые игры is broader — it encompasses non-BDSM fantasy scenarios (doctor/patient, teacher/student, strangers) and does not inherently involve power exchange.

definition: Cross-dressing; the practice of wearing clothing conventionally associated with a gender other than one's own, for any reason including gender expression, performance, or sexual arousal.
notes: Direct phonetic loanword from English; preferred in LGBTQ+-aware and progressive discourse as a neutral descriptor. The native alternative переодевание в одежду другого пола is unwieldy, driving adoption of the loanword. Carries fewer pathologising connotations than трансвестизм.

definition: Transvestism; the clinical/psychiatric term for wearing clothing associated with the opposite sex, whether for sexual gratification, gender expression, or performance.
notes: Standard Russian spelling is трансвестизм (no hyphen; the user's input 'транс-вестизм' is non-standard). More clinical and pathologising in connotation than кроссдрессинг; carries legacy DSM framing. LGBTQ+ discourse in Russia increasingly prefers кроссдрессинг to avoid medicalisation.
